'''Kathy Niakan''' is a developmental biologist, working in human developmental and stem cell biology. In 2016 she became the first scientist in the world to gain regulatory approval to edit the genomes of human embryos for research.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Callaway|first1=Ewen|title=UK scientists gain licence to edit genes in human embryos|journal=Nature|date=2016|volume=530|issue=7588|pages=18|doi=10.1038/nature.2016.19270|pmid=26842037|bibcode=2016Natur.530...18C|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Niakan was named as one of the 100 most influential people in the world by [[Time (magazine)|Time magazine]] in April 2016.<ref name="Time">{{Cite web|url=http://time.com/4301356/kathy-niakan-2016-time-100/|title=Kathy Niakan|last=Doudna|first=Jennfer|date=2016-04-21|website=The World’s 100 Most Influential People|publisher=Time Magazine|access-date=2016-06-11}}</ref>

==Biography==
Kathy Niakan obtained a BSc in cell and molecular biology and a BA in English literature from the [[University of Washington]]. In 2005, Niakan obtained her PhD in stem cell and developmental biology from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], where she worked in the laboratory of Edward McCabe.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.crick.ac.uk/research/find-a-researcher/kathy-niakan|title=Kathy Niakan|website=Crick|language=en|access-date=2019-02-15}}</ref> She went on to be a research fellow with [[Kevin Eggan]] at [[Harvard University]], working with human and mouse stem cells to study [[human embryogenesis]] and [[cell potency]]. She then moved to the [[University of Cambridge]] Anne McLaren Laboratory for Stem Cell Biology in the [[Cambridge Biomedical Campus]] where she continued to investigate the molecular basis of early cell development in humans and mice.<ref name="KN biog"/>
In 2013, Niakan became a group leader at the [[Medical Research Council (UK)|MRC]] [[National Institute for Medical Research]] (NIMR) in London.  Since 2015, she has been a group leader at the [[Francis Crick Institute]],<ref name=":0" /> the successor institute to the NIMR.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.crick.ac.uk/about-us/our-history/our-founders|title=Our founders|website=Crick|language=en|access-date=2019-02-15}}</ref>

She was a finalist in the inaugural UK [[Blavatnik Awards for Young Scientists]] in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://blavatnikawards.org/honorees/profile/kathy-niakan/|title=Kathy Niakan {{!}} Blavatnik Awards for Young Scientists|website=blavatnikawards.org|access-date=2019-01-10}}</ref>

In 2021, Professor Kathy Niakan was appointed as an honorary group leader in the Epigenetics research program as part of the [[Babraham Institute]], the third person appointed to such a position.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Epigenetics programme welcomes Professor Kathy Niakan as honorary group leader {{!}} Babraham Institute|url=https://www.babraham.ac.uk/news/2021/09/epigenetics-programme-welcomes-professor-kathy-niakan-honorary-group-leader|access-date=2021-10-03|website=www.babraham.ac.uk}}</ref>

Niakan was awarded the Mary Lyon Medal by [[The Genetics Society]] in 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mary Lyon Medal 2025 Prof Kathy Niakan |url=https://genetics.org.uk/medals-and-prizes/2025-winners/mary-lyon-medal-2025-prof-kathy-niakan/ |access-date=2026-05-06 |website=Genetics Society |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==Research==
At the Francis Crick Institute, Niakan is investigating the mechanisms of lineage specification in human embryos and stem cells.<ref name="KN biog">{{cite web|title=Kathy Niakan: Biography|url=https://www.crick.ac.uk/research/a-z-researchers/researchers-k-o/kathy-niakan/biography/|website=Francis Crick Institute|accessdate=15 February 2016}}</ref>

In February 2016, Niakan was given the go-ahead by the UK Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority to genetically modify human embryos.  The embryos were to be destroyed after seven days.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Gallagher|first1=James|title=Scientists get 'gene editing' go-ahead|work=BBC News|date=February 2016|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-35459054|accessdate=15 February 2016}}</ref> She planned to use the [[CRISPR]] technique to answer questions like what genetic faults cause some women to miscarry, what causes infertility and what is crucial for a healthy embryo.<ref name="KN biog"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-36439260|title=Gene editing technique could transform future|last=Walsh|first=Fergus|date=2016-06-06|website=BBC News|access-date=2016-06-11}}</ref> In 2017 her lab published the first major study using CRISPR-Cas9 in human embryos in [[Nature (journal)|Nature]], demonstrating that the transcription factor [[Oct4]] is essential for fetal development.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fogarty|first1=Norah M. E.|last2=McCarthy|first2=Afshan|last3=Snijders|first3=Kirsten E.|last4=Powell|first4=Benjamin E.|last5=Kubikova|first5=Nada|last6=Blakeley|first6=Paul|last7=Lea|first7=Rebecca|last8=Elder|first8=Kay|last9=Wamaitha|first9=Sissy E.|date=2017-09-20|title=Genome editing reveals a role for OCT4 in human embryogenesis|journal=Nature|language=En|volume=550|issue=7674|pages=67–73|doi=10.1038/nature24033|pmid=28953884|pmc=5815497|bibcode=2017Natur.550...67F|issn=0028-0836}}</ref>

In addition to her research, Niakan has engaged with policy makers, funders and the public to provide expert advice on genome editing.{{Citation needed|date=March 2026}}
